1. Neurological examination to assess the extent of neurological deficits and establish a clinical baseline.
2. MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast as the most sensitive imaging modality to identify CNS lesions characteristic of lymphoma.

7. Performance status evaluation to guide further diagnostic and treatment decisions.

Induction Phase: Initiate high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy, as this is the mainstay of induction for primary CNS lymphoma. Primary CNS lymphoma is a rare but aggressive cancer that originates from lymphocytes within the central nervous system, most commonly affecting the brain but also the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and eyes. Lung cancer remains a leading health concern, but you can take steps to reduce your risk and catch it early.  

**Know the Risk Factors**  
- **Tobacco smoke** is the biggest risk factor. More than 50 cancer-causing compounds are in tobacco smoke. The more you smoke and the longer you smoke, the higher your risk.  
- **Secondhand smoke** also increases risk.  
- Other cancer-causing agents include **radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and air pollution** (fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide).  
- Risk is higher for those over 70, with prior chest radiation, or exposure to carcinogens.  
- Some people with no risk factors still develop lung cancer; experts continue to study why.  

**Prevention**  
- If you don’t smoke, don’t start. If you do smoke, quit. New lung tumors are less likely after quitting.  
- Ask your health care provider about counseling and medicines to help you quit.  
- Avoid exposure to secondhand smoke and known carcinogens.  

**Early Detection and Screening**  
- Lung cancer starts in lung cells. Regular screening can find it at its earliest, most treatable stage for those at high risk.  
- A **lung nodule** is a small mass in the lung. Most are not cancer. If found, your team will assess your risk, review images, and possibly perform a biopsy.  
- If a nodule is unlikely to be cancer, you may be referred for lung cancer screening.  
- Ask your care team if you are eligible for screening and if a clinical trial is right for you.  

**Symptom Awareness**  
- Symptoms depend on where the tumor is or has spread. Lung cancer can prevent lungs from getting enough air.  
- Early and locally advanced NSCLC (stages 1–3) has not spread to the tissue lining around the lung or other organs.  
- Cancers that spread to the lungs from elsewhere are not lung cancer.  
- Be aware of persistent cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, or other unusual symptoms, and report them promptly.  

**Be Your Own Advocate**  
- You are an important member of your cancer care team. Discuss recommendations with your team and make a care plan that’s best for you.  
- Ask questions and make decisions with your team to get the care you want.

Staging is crucial: early-stage disease remains confined to the esophagus without lymph node involvement, while locoregional disease involves invasion of the esophageal wall and/or spread to regional lymph nodes or adjacent organs. Metastatic disease is defined by distant spread, particularly to the liver, lung, bone, or brain. The diagnostic workup includes blood tests, imaging (such as CT or PET scans), endoscopic evaluation with biopsy for histopathological confirmation, biomarker testing, and assessment of genetic risk factors. For tumors at the esophagogastric junction, Siewert classification assists in accurate staging. A comprehensive case summary for a newly diagnosed esophageal cancer patient should include the following:  

**Cancer Subtype Differentiation**: Esophageal cancer has two main subtypes. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) arises from thin, flat cells in the inner lining, commonly in the upper and middle esophagus but can occur in the lower esophagus. Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) arises from mucus-making cells and is often found in the lower esophagus but can occur in the middle esophagus. EAC is now the most common type in North America and Western Europe, whereas ESCC is more common in Eastern Europe, Asia, and Africa.  

**Staging Considerations**: Staging is grouped into three main categories: early-stage cancer (confined to the inside of the esophagus, tumor ≤2 cm, no lymph node involvement); locoregional or locally advanced cancer (invasion of the esophagus wall and/or spread to nearby lymph nodes or organs); and metastatic cancer (spread to distant sites, most commonly liver, distant lymph nodes, lung, bone, and brain). Siewert types are used to describe tumor location relative to the esophagogastric junction (EGJ), especially for tumors crossing from the stomach into the esophagus.  

**Diagnostic Workup**: The workup includes general health tests, nutritional assessment, blood tests, imaging tests, endoscopy procedures, biopsy, biomarker testing, genetic risk testing, and performance status evaluation. Results from blood tests, imaging studies, and biopsy are used for diagnosis and staging. Treatment planning starts with these tests.  

**Initial Factors for Treatment Planning**: Treatment is based on the type and location of the esophageal cancer, in addition to the tumor stage. Tumors that start in the stomach and cross into the esophagogastric junction may be treated as esophageal cancers rather than stomach cancers, depending on the exact location. Clinical practice guidelines, such as those available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app, should be referenced for management.  

Additional relevant clinical details include that the esophagus wall has four main layers (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, tunica adventitia), cancers tend to develop slowly with precancerous changes in the mucosa, and Barrett esophagus involves replacement of squamous cells in the lower esophagus, which is a risk factor for adenocarcinoma.

**Treatment Plan for a 32-Year-Old with Stage IB1 Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Cervix Desiring Fertility Preservation**

**1. Diagnostic Confirmation and Staging**
- **Histologic confirmation:** Review outside biopsy slides or perform repeat biopsy to confirm squamous cell carcinoma and grade. For stage IB1, the tumor is clinically visible and ≤2 cm (per FIGO 2018; note that the provided text defines IB2 as 2–4 cm and IB3 as >4 cm, implying IB1 is ≤2 cm).
- **Physical examination:** Thorough pelvic exam with speculum and rectovaginal palpation to assess tumor size, vaginal extension, and parametrial involvement.
- **Imaging:**  
  - **Pelvic MRI** (preferred) to accurately measure tumor size, assess cervical stroma invasion, vaginal/parametrial extension, and rule out bladder/rectal involvement.  
  - **Chest X-ray or CT chest** and **PET-CT** (or CT abdomen/pelvis) to evaluate for nodal and distant metastases.  
  - **Exam under anesthesia** with cystoscopy and proctoscopy if clinical suspicion of advanced local disease.
- **Staging:** Assign FIGO stage (IB1) and TNM stage. Document LVSI status if available from biopsy (though definitive LVSI is often assessed on surgical specimen).

**2. Multidisciplinary Consultation**
- Refer to a **reproductive endocrinologist** and **fertility counselor** before initiating treatment, as recommended in the provided text. Discuss fertility preservation options (oocyte/embryo cryopreservation, ovarian tissue cryopreservation) and the potential need for ovarian transposition if radiation becomes necessary.
- Discuss risks of fertility-sparing surgery: recurrence risk, need for completion hysterectomy, preterm birth, and cervical incompetence.

**3. Treatment Options for Stage IB1 with Fertility Preservation**
- **Fertility-sparing surgery:**  
  - **Radical trachelectomy** (abdominal, vaginal, or minimally invasive) with **pelvic lymph node dissection** (or sentinel lymph node mapping) is the standard for stage IB1 tumors ≤2 cm. This removes the cervix and upper vagina but preserves the uterine corpus and ovaries, allowing future pregnancy.  
  - **Cone biopsy** is generally not adequate for stage IB1 (visible lesion), except in very select low-risk cases (e.g., stage IA2), but the text notes cone biopsy is recommended for stage 1A1 without LVSI. For IB1, radical trachelectomy is preferred.  
  - **Abdominal radical trachelectomy** is often preferred for tumors >2 cm or when abdominal approach is favored, as the provided text states for stage 1B2 "abdominal surgery is generally preferred" due to research on smaller tumors. For IB1 (≤2 cm), vaginal or minimally invasive approaches may be considered at high-volume centers.
- **Pelvic lymph node evaluation:** Always performed (sentinel node biopsy or full lymphadenectomy). If nodes are positive, fertility-sparing surgery is generally abandoned, and chemoradiation is recommended.
- **If fertility-sparing surgery is not feasible** (e.g., positive nodes, positive margins, or patient choice):  
  - **Radical hysterectomy** with pelvic lymph node dissection (and possible para-aortic sampling).  
  - **Adjuvant therapy:** Based on risk factors (tumor size, LVSI, depth of invasion, nodal status), EBRT with or without platinum-based chemoradiation may be recommended, as stated in the text: "If EBRT is planned, platinum chemotherapy may be given during the same time period." Vaginal brachytherapy may be added.
- **If surgery is contraindicated:** Definitive **chemoradiation** with external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) plus brachytherapy is recommended, but this eliminates fertility. Therefore, fertility preservation must be addressed before treatment.

**4. Fertility Preservation Strategies**
- **Oocyte/embryo cryopreservation:** Before surgery, controlled ovarian hyperstimulation and retrieval can be performed. For squamous cell carcinoma, ovarian stimulation is generally safe (unlike some hormone-sensitive tumors).  
- **Ovarian transposition:** If radiation is planned, laparoscopically move ovaries out of the radiation field to preserve endocrine function, though this does not preserve fertility if uterus is irradiated.  
- **Reproductive endocrinologist referral:** As stated in the text, "ask your doctor about getting the opinion of a reproductive endocrinologist."  
- **Post-treatment surveillance:** After radical trachelectomy, regular Pap smears and imaging. Pregnancy should be managed by a high-risk obstetrician due to risk of preterm birth and cervical incompetence (may require cerclage).

**5. Surveillance and Follow-Up**
- Every 3–4 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3–5 years: pelvic exam, cytology, and imaging as clinically indicated.
- Monitor for recurrence, especially at the trachelectomy site or pelvic nodes.

**6. Key Guideline References**
- NCCN Guidelines for Cervical Cancer (fertility-sparing surgery for stage IB1 ≤2 cm; radical trachelectomy with lymph node assessment).
- The provided text supports: "Fertility-sparing treatment may be an option, if desired, for some stage 1 cancers. This approach involves surgery that does not remove the uterus or ovaries, allowing you the option of natural pregnancy in the future."
- Also: "For stage 1A1 cancers with LVSI, treatment with either cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy is recommended. Pelvic lymph node evaluation should also be performed." (Extrapolate to IB1 for lymph node evaluation.)
- "Fertility-sparing surgery is not performed often for stage 1B2 cancers... abdominal surgery is generally preferred." (For IB1, fertility-sparing is more feasible but still requires careful selection.)

**Conclusion:** Offer radical trachelectomy with pelvic lymph node assessment as the primary fertility-sparing option, after confirming no nodal metastasis. Preoperative fertility preservation (oocyte/embryo cryopreservation) and reproductive endocrinology consultation are essential. If nodal or margin positivity is found, proceed with hysterectomy and adjuvant chemoradiation, with prior fertility counseling.

Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a common, slow-growing (indolent) non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that arises from mature B cells. Key features: excess abnormal B lymphocytes cluster into follicles in germinal centers; most cases involve a chromosome translocation or excess BCL2 protein. Grading matters: ICC classifies grades 1–2 as classic FL; WHO5 also includes grade 3A as classic FL. Grade 3A may be treated as classic FL or DLBCL depending on the center and cell testing. Primary care providers should suspect FL in patients with persistent, unexplained swollen lymph nodes, enlarged nodes, or extranodal symptoms (e.g., bone marrow involvement). Diagnostic workup includes: general health and blood tests, fertility assessment (all genders) and pregnancy prevention during treatment, performance status, biopsy with immunophenotyping, testing for FL biomarkers and genetic changes (e.g., BCL2, chromosome translocation), imaging tests, and heart tests.

- Consider primary bone cancer in patients presenting with persistent, unexplained bone pain (especially at night or with activity), localized swelling, a palpable mass, or pathologic fracture.

- **History and physical exam:** Document all health issues, treatments, and current medications/supplements.

Imaging tests, such as CT or MRI, will assess the extent of disease, including invasion into stomach wall layers and potential spread to regional lymph nodes or distant organs like the liver or peritoneum. Based on the provided guideline, the diagnostic workup for suspected stomach cancer should proceed as follows:

1. **Clinical evaluation and history**: Assess for symptoms that may indicate an ulcer or mass, as stomach cancer can grow inward and form lesions that cause symptoms. However, note that early precancerous changes and early-stage tumors rarely cause symptoms and often go undetected. This step helps determine the need for further testing but cannot alone diagnose or stage the disease.

2. **Upper endoscopy with biopsy**: Perform endoscopy to visualize the inner lining (mucosa) of the stomach and obtain biopsies. This is essential because most stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas starting in the mucus-producing cells lining the stomach. Biopsy confirms malignancy and distinguishes intestinal type (cells sticking together, forming tube- and gland-shaped structures, more likely to have treatable mutations) from diffuse type (scattered cells, less common). This histologic classification directly guides treatment selection, including targeted therapy for intestinal-type tumors.

3. **Biomarker testing**: On biopsy specimens, test for mutations that can be treated with targeted therapy, particularly relevant for intestinal-type adenocarcinomas. This informs systemic treatment options.

4. **Imaging and staging studies**: Use imaging to determine the extent of spread, which defines the three main categories:  
   - **Early-stage**: cancer not grown beyond the mucosa; tumor often small (≤2 cm) and not in lymph nodes.  
   - **Locoregional or locally advanced**: cancer invaded other layers of the stomach wall (submucosa or beyond) and/or spread to regional lymph nodes or nearby organs.  
   - **Metastatic**: cancer spread to distant sites, most commonly liver, peritoneum, distant lymph nodes, and possibly lungs or bone.  
   Relevant imaging may include CT, PET, and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) to assess wall layers, lymph nodes, and distant metastases. The guideline notes that stomach cancers can spread to nearby lymph nodes, veins, arteries, and organs such as liver, pancreas, and spleen, and can grow into lymphatic or blood vessels. Staging imaging should evaluate these areas.

5. **Assess tumor location**: Determine if the tumor starts in the cardia of the stomach and crosses into the esophagogastric junction. Such tumors are treated as esophageal cancers, so the workup and treatment should follow esophageal cancer guidelines, including appropriate staging and management.

6. **Multidisciplinary treatment planning**: Integrate results from endoscopy, biopsy, biomarker testing, and imaging to classify the cancer by stage (early, locoregional, metastatic) and type (intestinal vs. diffuse). Treatment is based on the type of stomach cancer and the location of the tumor. For example, early-stage disease may be amenable to local resection, while locoregional disease may require surgery plus lymph node dissection and/or systemic therapy, and metastatic disease requires systemic therapy. The guideline emphasizes that treatment planning starts with testing, so all diagnostic steps should be completed before finalizing therapy.

Rationale for each step: Endoscopy and biopsy establish diagnosis and histologic subtype; biomarker testing identifies targeted therapy options; imaging stages the disease and detects metastases; location assessment distinguishes stomach from esophageal cancer management. SOAP Progress Note for Low-Grade Astrocytoma

Subjective:
Patient may present with or without symptoms. Common symptoms include unusual or frequent headaches, seizures, changes in personality or mood, nausea and vomiting, difficulty speaking or swallowing, muscle weakness, and difficulty with walking, balance, or coordination. Some patients with low-grade gliomas never have symptoms; tumors can grow slowly for years before diagnosis. Symptoms, when present, relate to tumor location and size, often due to pressure on the brain or invasion of brain tissue. Patient may report insidious onset affecting personality, language, memory, or physical function. History should include any prior illnesses, injuries, treatments, and timing of symptom onset.

Objective:
General health examination and thorough neurologic evaluation. Imaging (e.g., MRI) typically shows a mass in the upper part of the brain with vague borders, blending into normal tissue. Tissue sample from biopsy or resection is evaluated by neuropathologist. Astrocytoma resembles astrocytes (star-shaped glial cells). Grade determined by how much tumor cells look like normal cells: grade 1 (slow-growing, usually benign, more common in children) or grade 2 (cells somewhat abnormal, grow slowly, can invade normal tissue). Biomarker testing on tissue sample identifies mutations in genes, proteins, and other markers to improve diagnostic accuracy and guide prognosis. No distinct well-defined edges are common; tumor cells may be left behind to avoid damaging nearby brain tissue.

Assessment:
Low-grade astrocytoma (grade 1 or 2). Grade 1 tumors grow slowly and are usually benign; many can be treated with surgery alone, but if tumor grows back, additional therapy may be given. Grade 2 tumors grow slowly, can invade normal tissue, and may not grow back for many years; however, when they do recur, they usually return as a higher-grade glioma. Each glioma has unique molecular characteristics and behavior. Prognosis is generally better than high-grade gliomas, but long-term surveillance is essential due to risk of recurrence and malignant transformation. Differential diagnosis includes other glioma types (oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma) and non-neoplastic lesions; histopathology and biomarker testing confirm diagnosis.

Plan:
1. Diagnosis: Confirm via tissue sampling (biopsy or surgical resection) with neuropathologic evaluation and biomarker testing.
2. Management: For grade 1 astrocytoma, surgical resection alone is often curative; if tumor grows back, consider additional therapy. For grade 2 astrocytoma, maximal safe surgical resection is first-line; consider postoperative radiation and/or chemotherapy for high-risk features (e.g., incomplete resection, age, molecular markers) or at recurrence.
3. Surveillance: Regular clinical follow-up and serial MRI imaging to monitor for recurrence or progression to higher-grade glioma. Frequency individualized based on grade, molecular profile, and residual disease. Monitor for new or worsening symptoms (headaches, seizures, personality/mood changes, language/memory impairment, motor weakness, balance/coordination issues).
4. Supportive care: Symptom management (antiepileptics for seizures, corticosteroids for edema, antiemetics for nausea). Referral to neuro-oncology, rehabilitation, and psychosocial support as needed.
5. Patient education: Discuss unique nature of each glioma, importance of adherence to surveillance, and potential for late recurrence or transformation. Encourage bringing someone to appointments to listen, ask questions, and write down answers.

Laboratory and Molecular Diagnostic Report:

A diagnosis of AML requires identification of ≥20% myeloblasts in bone marrow or blood. The diagnostic process began with complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to evaluate cytopenias and cell turnover. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy were performed, with histopathology confirming increased blasts. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping defined the immunologic profile of the blasts. Cytogenetic analysis (karyotype, FISH) and molecular testing (next-generation sequencing, PCR) were conducted to identify genetic alterations such as FLT3-ITD, inv(16), t(8;21), del(5q), and PML::RARA. These findings are essential for AML subtype classification and to guide therapy.

1. Initial laboratory evaluation: Complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, B12, folate, and blood clotting tests to assess cytopenias, metabolic complications, and coagulopathy.

2. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy: Essential for diagnosis. Morphologic review quantifies myeloid blasts (myeloblasts). In general, AML is diagnosed when ≥20% myeloblasts are present in bone marrow or blood; however, any blast percentage can be diagnostic if specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are present.

3. Immunophenotyping: Flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry on aspirate/biopsy to confirm myeloid lineage and identify blast immunophenotype, aiding subtype classification.

4. Cytogenetic analysis: Karyotyping and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on bone marrow or blood to detect recurrent chromosomal abnormalities that define AML subtypes and risk.

5. Molecular genetic testing: AML biomarker and genetic tests, including mutation analysis for genes such as NPM1, FLT3, CEBPA, IDH1/2, RUNX1, TP53, and others, plus fusion gene detection, to define subtype, target therapy, and determine prognosis.

6. Additional testing as clinically indicated: HLA typing if hematopoietic cell transplant is considered; lumbar puncture if CNS involvement is suspected (leukemic meningitis) or to detect leukemia cells in spinal fluid; brain CT/MRI or FDG-PET/CT for suspected extramedullary or CNS disease; heart tests before anthracycline or transplant therapy; fertility assessment and performance status evaluation.

7. Integration and reporting: A clinical pathologist integrates morphologic, immunophenotypic, cytogenetic, and molecular findings to confirm AML, assign the WHO subtype, and provide prognostic and predictive information to guide treatment.

Public Health Advisory: Early Recognition and Referral for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

Primary care providers should maintain high suspicion for AML in patients presenting with unexplained fatigue, frequent infections, bleeding, or easy bruising. Risk factors include family history of leukemia and hereditary predisposition syndromes. Early diagnosis relies on prompt laboratory evaluation, including complete blood count and referral for bone marrow assessment if blasts are detected. Rapid referral to hematology is essential for definitive diagnosis and initiation of therapy. Fertility preservation counseling should be considered before starting systemic treatment. Supportive care, including transfusions and infection prevention, is critical during initial management.

Public Health Advisory: Early Recognition and Referral for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

To: Primary Care Providers

Key Points:
- AML is a life-threatening blood cancer that is fatal if left untreated.
- Early recognition and prompt referral are critical to improve patient outcomes.

Early Recognition:
- Consider AML in patients presenting with symptoms of bone marrow failure: fatigue, pallor, infections, easy bruising or bleeding.
- Order a complete blood count (CBC) with differential. AML may present with abnormal counts, including blasts (immature white blood cells) that crowd out normal blood cells.
- Be aware that AML has many subtypes, including acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which is associated with the abnormal fusion gene PML::RARA, and blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN), which can involve blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and/or skin.

Risk Factors:
- Certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are associated with AML subtypes.
- APL is characterized by the PML::RARA fusion gene.
- BPDCN is an aggressive subtype that may present with skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, or abnormal blood counts.

Referral Pathways:
- Refer urgently to a hematologist or hematologic oncologist for suspected AML.
- Consider seeking the opinion of an AML specialist.
- Treatment should involve a multidisciplinary team (MDT) including hematologic oncologists, medical oncologists, pathologists, and psychosocial care professionals.
- Accurate testing—including blood tests, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, genetic and biomarker mutation testing, and imaging—is needed to diagnose and guide treatment.

Providers should advocate for shared decision-making with patients and use trusted resources such as the NCCN Guidelines for Patients to support care discussions. Early referral to specialized care can improve outcomes.

CLL is predominantly found in the blood and bone marrow, whereas SLL is predominantly found in the lymph nodes and spleen. A lymphocyte count of fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells in the blood is classified as SLL; a count exceeding this threshold is classified as CLL. Lymph nodes and spleen may be swollen due to buildup of CLL/SLL cells. CLL/SLL is a slowly growing blood cancer; treatment may not be needed for years, and some patients may never require treatment. There is currently no cure, but effective treatment can achieve minimal residual disease and prevent life-threatening complications. A rare complication, Richter transformation, can lead to a more aggressive cancer such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or Hodgkin lymphoma.

**Risk Factors:** Disease progression and the potential development of Richter transformation. Higher risk levels on specific tests may suggest that CLL will be harder to treat. The clinical course varies greatly from person to person.

**Follow-Up Strategy:** The patient will be managed with "watch and wait," which involves monitoring without active treatment unless symptoms or disease progression warrant intervention. No treatment will be initiated aside from supportive care measures to improve quality of life. Follow-up will include regular assessments to determine if and when treatment should begin, based on test results and clinical status. If Richter transformation is suspected or diagnosed, the patient will be referred for management of this rare and more aggressive complication. The patient is encouraged to ask questions, advocate for themselves, and participate in shared decision-making with the care team.

**Supportive Care Advice:** Supportive care should be provided to improve quality of life. The patient should maintain regular communication with the care team, bring a family member to appointments to take notes, and ask as many questions as possible. The patient should refer to the NCCN Guidelines for Patients for a better understanding of cancer care and to reduce anxiety. Any recommendations for CLL also apply to SLL, as the cancer cells are the same.

I also learned that Trodelvy (sacituzumab govitecan-hziy) targets Trop-2, another protein found on bladder cancer cells, but my team felt Padcev was the better fit right now.

Because my cancer is metastatic, my oncologist recommended systemic therapy. The preferred regimen for metastatic bladder cancer is a combination of a targeted therapy (Padcev) and an immunotherapy (Keytruda/pembrolizumab). I receive both intravenously. Padcev seeks out and attaches to Nectin-4 on cancer cells, while Keytruda is a checkpoint inhibitor that blocks the natural braking mechanisms in my immune system so it can better identify and fight the cancer. I also had a TURBT (transurethral resection of bladder tumor) initially to remove visible tumors from my bladder wall, and I may need radiation therapy (external beam radiation, EBRT) later if specific spots cause pain or bleeding. I understand that most people with bladder cancer require more than one type of treatment over months or years, and that treatment is based on the extent of the cancer, my overall health, and my personal wishes.

The side effects have been challenging. From Padcev, I’ve experienced fatigue and some peripheral neuropathy (numbness in my hands and feet). From Keytruda, I’ve had skin rash and mild diarrhea. - Imaging (CT scans of chest, abdomen, and pelvis) every few months
- Blood and urine tests to monitor organ function and look for cancer markers
- Inherited cancer risk assessment, which I completed and found no additional hereditary mutations
- Quitting smoking (which I have done) to reduce the risk of recurrence and improve treatment outcomes

Kidney cancer encompasses several types, most commonly renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which originates in the renal tubules, and urothelial carcinoma, starting in the renal pelvis or ureter. Wilms tumor is the predominant form in young children. Early detection is crucial, as kidney cancer can locally invade surrounding fat, blood vessels, lymph nodes, and adrenal glands, and can metastasize to the lungs, bones, liver, and brain. Diagnosis often requires imaging, blood and urine tests, biopsy, and biomarker/genetic risk assessments. Recognizing risk factors and symptoms, and pursuing timely diagnostic evaluation, can improve outcomes.

Less common kidney cancers include urothelial carcinoma (starting in the renal pelvis and ureter), Wilms tumor in young children, and renal sarcoma.

Importance of early detection: Early detection supports accurate diagnosis and timely treatment based on tumor size, subtype, location, and spread. Because sarcomatoid RCC grows quickly and is more likely to spread, and because metastatic disease can involve distant organs, early recognition is important for effective management.

Anal cancer rates are increasing, particularly among individuals with certain risk factors. HPV vaccination and smoking cessation are strongly encouraged for prevention. Consult your healthcare provider if you have risk factors or symptoms.

Pancreatic cancer is a serious disease that often presents late due to subtle symptoms. Risk factors include smoking, heavy alcohol use, unhealthy diet, exposure to pesticides, diabetes, chronic pancreatitis, and family history of pancreatic, breast, ovarian, colorectal, or melanoma cancers. Pancreatic cancer is a complex disease that begins when cells in the pancreas grow uncontrollably and form a tumor. It can spread to nearby tissues and other parts of the body. Because early pancreatic cancer often has no clear symptoms, community awareness and timely medical evaluation are critical.

Who is at higher risk?
- Lifestyle factors: smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, and a less healthy diet.
- Environmental/occupational exposure: major contact with cancer-causing chemicals, such as pesticides.
- Health conditions: diabetes and chronic inflammation of the pancreas.
- Family history: close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma.

What signs should prompt medical attention?
- Jaundice: yellowing of the skin or eyes.
- Other possible signs may be caused by different health conditions, which is why testing is needed. On imaging, doctors may see wider-than-normal pancreatic ducts or an inflamed pancreas.
- There is no tell-tale early sign, so anyone with concerning symptoms or strong risk factors should seek care promptly.

Why early diagnosis matters
- A series of tests is needed to identify pancreatic cancer and make a treatment plan. Imaging is key to staging the cancer and deciding if surgery is an option.

- Some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer can have surgery to remove the cancer. Surgery is an option for more people now than in the past due to medical advances.
- Stage 4 pancreatic cancer is metastatic, meaning it has spread far from the pancreas, commonly to the liver, lungs, or lining of the abdomen.

- Reduce modifiable risks: avoid tobacco, limit alcohol, eat a healthier diet, and minimize exposure to cancer-causing chemicals.

**Public Health Advisory: Prostate Cancer Awareness for Men Over 50**

Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers among men. Early stages are often asymptomatic, making screening crucial for early detection. Risk increases with age, family history, Black race, and genetic mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2. Lifestyle factors including obesity, smoking, and high-fat diets may also elevate risk. Screening methods include the PSA blood test and digital rectal exam; abnormal results should be evaluated by a healthcare professional. Diagnosis is confirmed with a prostate biopsy and may include imaging such as MRI or ultrasound to determine disease extent. Treatment options vary by stage and risk group, ranging from active surveillance for low-risk cases to surgery, radiation, hormone therapy, and chemotherapy for more advanced disease. Regular follow-up with PSA testing and imaging is important for all men diagnosed with prostate cancer.

- If you are over 50, talk to your doctor about prostate cancer screening.
- If diagnosed, seek care or a second opinion from a medical center that specializes in prostate cancer.

**Public Health Notice: Breast Cancer Awareness, Screening, and Early Detection**

Breast cancer is a disease that can affect anyone, though it occurs much more frequently in individuals assigned female at birth. Understanding risk factors, recommended screening practices, and the importance of early detection is critical for reducing deaths from breast cancer.

**Risk Factors**
- Most breast cancers have no clear cause or risk factor, but family history and inherited gene mutations can increase risk.
- A personal or family history of breast cancer or related syndromes (such as familial adenomatous polyposis, Carney complex, Cowden syndrome/PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, or multiple endocrine neoplasia) may elevate risk.
- Anyone can develop breast cancer, including those assigned male at birth.
- Sharing a complete medical and family history with your care team—including specific cancer types, age at diagnosis, and any genetic testing—helps determine the best screening and treatment approach.

**Screening**
- Breast cancer screening aims to find cancer early, before symptoms start. Early detection leads to more successful treatment and reduces the risk of dying from breast cancer.
- Screening mammograms are performed regularly when there are no signs or symptoms. They use low-dose x-rays (2D digital mammography or 3D tomosynthesis) and results typically take a few days.
- Diagnostic mammograms are used for individuals with symptoms such as a lump, pain, nipple thickening or discharge, or changes in breast shape or size. A radiologist evaluates these immediately so additional testing can be done right away.
- Screening recommendations apply to those assigned female at birth. Screening and testing options are also available for those who are pregnant or lactating, and for those with breast pain, nipple discharge, skin changes, lumps, or other symptoms requiring further testing.

**Importance of Early Detection**
- Breast cancer found earlier is treated more successfully. Screening saves lives by detecting cancer at an earlier, more treatable stage.
- Metastatic breast cancer (also called advanced breast cancer) has spread to other parts of the body, underscoring the value of catching breast cancer before it spreads.
- If you notice any changes in your breasts—such as a lump, skin changes, or nipple discharge—seek evaluation promptly, even if you feel silly asking for testing for a small bump.

**Recommended Practices**
- Know your personal and family health history, including heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age relatives were diagnosed.
- Bring a list of all medicines, over-the-counter drugs, herbals, and supplements to your care team, as some can interact with prescribed treatments.
- Follow recommended screening schedules and discuss any symptoms or concerns with your primary care provider or specialist.

For more information, refer to the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Breast Cancer – Ductal Carcinoma In Situ, Breast Cancer – Invasive, and Breast Cancer – Metastatic, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines. Early detection saves lives.

per_example.question: Transform the clinical facts on metastatic breast cancer (MBC) into a structured SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) progress note for a follow-up visit. Include relevant symptoms, diagnostics, biomarkers, and ongoing management.
per_example.gold:
SOAP Progress Note

Subjective: Patient reports persistent bone pain and intermittent shortness of breath. No new neurological symptoms or liver dysfunction.

Objective: Imaging tests (PET scan) confirm metastases to bone and lung. Blood tests within normal limits. Biopsy confirms metastatic breast cancer. Biomarker analysis reveals hormone receptor positivity (ER/PR+) and HER2 negativity. Performance status remains stable.

Assessment: Stage IV metastatic breast cancer with bone and pulmonary involvement, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative.

Plan: Continue systemic therapy with endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitor. Monitor for disease progression with regular imaging and physical exams. Manage bone metastases with bisphosphonates. Provide supportive care for symptom control. Discuss ongoing eligibility for targeted therapies.

Clinical lymph node involvement may include axillary, internal mammary, infraclavicular, or supraclavicular nodes.

- Metastatic breast cancer (MBC), also called advanced breast cancer, stage IV.
- Cancer has spread from primary breast tumor to distant sites via blood or lymph vessels.
- Most common sites of metastasis: bone and lung.
- Grade and receptor status inform prognosis and treatment.
- Cancer is still called breast cancer despite metastasis to other parts of body.

- Monitoring and follow-up care as outlined in Part 6: When treatment is over.
- Patient education on metastatic disease, recurrence risk, and symptom reporting.

per_example.question: Assume the role of a genetic counselor. Prepare a summary for a patient newly found to have a BRCA1 mutation, explaining the implications for breast cancer risk, recommended surveillance, and potential preventive strategies.
per_example.gold:
Genetic Counseling Summary:

You have tested positive for a BRCA1 mutation, which significantly increases your risk of developing breast cancer. Having a BRCA1 mutation is a strong risk factor and may also impact your family members’ risk. We recommend enhanced surveillance, including annual mammograms and breast MRI starting at an earlier age. Preventive strategies may include risk-reducing medications or prophylactic surgery (such as bilateral mastectomy or oophorectomy). It is important to discuss these options with your oncology and surgical teams. Family members may also wish to consider genetic testing. Ongoing follow-up and support resources are available to you.
per_example.pred_answer: As your genetic counselor, I want to help you understand what a BRCA1 mutation means for your health. Everyone has BRCA genes, which normally help prevent tumor growth by repairing damaged cells. A BRCA1 mutation is an inherited (germline) change that raises your risk for several cancers, especially breast and ovarian cancer, as well as prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, and melanoma skin cancers. For breast cancer, this means your lifetime risk is significantly higher than average. Because BRCA1 mutations can be passed to children and may affect other family members, I recommend discussing family history and considering testing for blood relatives. For surveillance, your care team will likely recommend regular breast imaging, including diagnostic mammogram, ultrasound, and breast MRI as needed, along with clinical breast exams. You should also address fertility, birth control, and sexual health concerns with your providers. Potential preventive strategies may include enhanced screening, risk-reducing medications, or risk-reducing surgery such as bilateral mastectomy and/or salpingo-oophorectomy, depending on your age, family plans, and personal preferences. BRCA status can also guide treatment if cancer is diagnosed. I encourage you to continue working with a multidisciplinary team and to ask about genetic counseling for relatives. We will tailor all decisions to your individual situation.
